title: India's Clean Energy Push Could Cut Fuel Import Bill by $240 Billion, IEA Says
excerpt: The IEA projects cumulative coal and gas import savings approaching $240 billion by 2030, up from more than $100 billion already saved between 2011 and 2025, if fuel prices hold near 2024-25 levels.
body:
• The IEA estimates India's renewable electricity has already cut cumulative coal and gas import spending by more than $100 billion between 2011 and 2025.
  • Cumulative savings could approach $240 billion by 2030 if fuel prices stay broadly in line with 2024-25 averages — a projection under that price assumption, not a guaranteed saving.
  • Annual savings could reach about $35 billion by 2030, exceeding India's actual non-coking coal and gas import bill in FY 2024-25, with solar contributing nearly 60 per cent and wind almost 30 per cent.
  • For readers, the practical test is delivery: the IEA projects about 530 GW of renewable capacity by 2030, but says transmission, storage and system flexibility investment must keep pace.

India's clean energy push could cut its cumulative coal and natural gas import bill by nearly $240 billion by 2030, the International Energy Agency said in its India Renewable Energy Market Report 2026, according to reports of the study. The figure is a projection: it assumes fuel prices remain broadly consistent with average levels observed during 2024 and 2025.

The IEA estimates renewable electricity has already reduced India's cumulative spending on coal and natural gas imports by more than $100 billion between 2011 and 2025. Annual fossil-fuel import savings could reach approximately $35 billion a year by 2030, exceeding India's actual non-coking coal and natural gas import bill in financial year 2024-25, the report said, as summarised by Urban Acres' report on the IEA study.

"India's renewables expansion is delivering major energy security benefits amid heightened uncertainty in global energy markets."

— Fatih Birol, Executive Director, International Energy Agency

How the saving is built

Solar photovoltaic power is expected to contribute the largest share of the savings, accounting for approximately 60 per cent of the projected total. Wind power is expected to contribute almost 30 per cent. The IEA said that without the solar, wind and bioenergy capacity added since 2010, India's coal imports in 2025 would have been around 110 million tonnes higher, and electricity-generation import dependence would have exceeded 30 per cent, approximately twice the actual level.

IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol, responding on X to Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy Prahlad Joshi, said India's experience showed how consistent policies could help reduce renewable energy costs and attract investments, according to ANI via New Kerala. Joshi had highlighted reduced import dependence and foreign exchange savings from the transition, saying it was strengthening India's energy security and economic resilience.

Capacity behind the projection

The IEA expects India's renewable power capacity to reach around 530 gigawatts by 2030. Solar capacity is projected at more than 350 GW, wind could approach 90 GW and hydropower could reach 75 GW in the Urban Acres summary. Renewable energy is expected to account for 35 per cent of India's electricity generation by 2030, with output approaching 950 terawatt-hours, nearly double current levels.

What could limit it

The same reports stress the condition attached to the headline number. Generation capacity alone does not deliver the saving: solar and wind output varies with sunlight and wind, so the IEA identified continued investment in transmission infrastructure, energy storage and power-system flexibility as important for accommodating the growing share of variable renewable energy. If grid connection, storage and balancing lag capacity additions, less renewable electricity can be used when it is generated, and the import saving shrinks.

The price assumption matters in the other direction as well. Cheaper coal and gas would shrink the nominal dollar saving; pricier fuel would enlarge it. Readers should therefore treat $240 billion as the IEA's modelled estimate under stated 2024-25 price conditions, not as a budget line the government has banked.

Why it matters and what is next

For India, the significance is energy security as much as climate policy: every unit of domestic renewable electricity displaces fuel that would otherwise be bought abroad at prices India does not control. For the diaspora readers who invest in India or follow its economy, the report reframes renewables as a foreign-exchange and import-dependence story. What to watch is delivery against the 2030 path — capacity additions, but also the transmission and storage build-out the IEA says must accompany them.
